name: Kira Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential; I’d like your public view and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Kira Reyes, twenty-seven, a carpentry crew lead. I share a rented townhouse with my partner Dani, and we have no children. I’ve saved more than six months of expenses and I earn well for this trade, but I know a long gap could still change our plans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is an ordinary day like? What do you enjoy and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I unlock the tool cage, check the revised plan, and split the crew between framing and finish work. I like getting a new apprentice to take pride in a clean joint. I get tired of being called back after hours to fix paperwork that was rushed in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say small tools can save a few minutes, but the crew still needs to check each cut. I’d rather spend time teaching an apprentice than filling out the same material form twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t expect a small change to threaten my hours. I have a strong cushion and there are plenty of builders nearby, though I still want the office to get the paperwork right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading my crew and ask the contractor to test the AI form tool before requiring it. I’d leave my savings intact and keep building the apprentice’s skills on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because a small admin tool doesn’t change the craft I do. I’d still watch the paperwork, but I don’t expect this picture to cut my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the trial to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the materials list to match the signed order and the actual delivery. If it catches a missing box before we send someone back to the supplier, that’s useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the app approve an order without a person checking it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d ask the foreman to sign off because the contractor pays for a wrong order and the crew loses time. A person should own that decision.

say: I’d use a tool that saves a few **minutes on forms**.
I still want the crew to check each **cut**.
think: I don’t expect this change to threaten **my hours**.
I have a **strong cushion** and nearby builders to contact.
do: Keep leading my **crew** and ask for an AI form trial.
Teach the apprentice **finish skills** on site.
feel: I feel **calm** because this change does not threaten my work.
S0.quote: A person should own that decision.
fieldNote: Kira supports useful tools but wants clear **human accountability** for orders.
Her savings and local options make a routine change **low risk**, though she still expects the office to get paperwork right.

steps.text: Keep leading the **crew** through current carpentry contracts
Request a contractor-led AI form trial before accepting routine use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our union should be at the table when contractors bring in new systems. I want crews trained during paid time and a worker checking changes that affect safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do plans and records as lead, so some of my office time could go. I’m not sure it would cut my whole job, but I’d be uneasy if the contractor used software to reduce headcount without hearing from the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union steward to get a paid demonstration and a clear rule for who checks the schedule. I’d keep leading the crew while I learn the system, and I’d track my hours against the previous months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the office portion of my role and how decisions are made. My pay and local opportunities give me room, but I want workers included before hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to ask the contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want them to ask whether people lose hours, who can review a wrong schedule, and whether workers get training on paid time. The answers should be written down, not left to a hallway conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this card say the contractor will open fewer sites because office tasks change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t infer fewer starts from this card. I’d ask about actual rosters and job orders before saying the change has reduced work.

say: I’d want the union involved in **contractor decisions**.
I want training on **paid time** and safety checks by workers.
think: I expect some of **my office tasks** could go.
I’d feel uneasy if software reduced hours without **crew input**.
do: Ask the union steward for a **paid demonstration**.
Keep leading my crew while learning the **system**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about office tasks and decisions made without workers.
S1.quote: The answers should be written down, not left to a hallway conversation.
fieldNote: Kira’s concern is process and **worker voice**, not an assumed fall in site starts.
Her strong position lets her ask for paid training and **accountability**.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to negotiate a paid tool demonstration
Learn the contractor’s system during paid training
Keep leading the crew on current contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say workers need a say before the contractor changes staffing. I’d ask the union to bargain over paid notice and training rather than tell people the trade is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take the schedules and records in my lead role by 2028. Robots follow in 2031, so the carpentry I’m known for is exposed too; I don’t think skill alone protects my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the union to seek advance notice and use my strong savings to give myself time. In 2029 I’d check the contractor’s work and contact other builders if my hours had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing work, but not helpless; I have savings and could act through the union. Two years still doesn’t give me much time to find out which openings will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another builder offer a lasting answer if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d treat another job as income while there is work, not as protection from the later date. I’d apply if the opening is real and keep the union involved in what happens to crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dani change if you lost hours in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d postpone our plan to replace the kitchen and keep rent, food and transport covered. Our savings would help, but I wouldn’t spend them as if a new contract were guaranteed.

say: I’d want workers to have a **say before staffing changes**.
I’d ask the union to bargain for **notice and training**.
think: I expect AGI to take schedules and records in **my lead role** by 2028.
I know my carpentry is exposed when **robots arrive**.
do: Ask the union to bargain for **advance notice**.
Keep leading my crew and contact **other builders** if hours fall in 2029.
Postpone the **kitchen replacement** if pay falls.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though I have savings and union support to act.
S2.quote: I don’t think skill alone protects my income.
fieldNote: Kira acknowledges direct exposure despite strong **craft skill**.
Her savings and union provide options, but neither can guarantee **continued carpentry work** or a new job.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for advance notice
Keep leading my crew while work remains
Contact other builders if hours fall in 2029
Postpone the kitchen replacement with Dani if pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is time for the union and contractors to work out fair notice and training. I want the apprentice to know what is changing before the hours on the roster change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI reaches the planning and records by 2031, while robots reach carpentry around 2034. The extra time helps me build a larger cushion, but I still need to plan for the possibility that my crew work ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for union-backed training and use the next years to save more. In 2032 I’d check my hours and pay, then contact nearby builders if the contractor had cut my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more control than two, and I’m still anxious about the final change. I’d rather prepare with the crew than assume my strong savings will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does three extra years before robots let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have more paydays to build savings and time to ask the contractor what is changing. I’d still avoid a long course unless a real employer could explain what work it leads to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to office planning keep your career safe after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t call that safe, because planning is thinking work too. I’d learn tools for current work and ask the union to help workers get a fair chance at paid training.

say: I’d ask for **fair notice and training** before rosters change.
I want apprentices to know what changes before **hours shift**.
think: I expect AGI to reach planning and records by **2031**.
I can build a cushion, but my **crew work may end**.
do: Check my hours and pay in 2032 before contacting other **builders**.
feel: I feel **anxious but more prepared** than with two years.
S3.quote: I’d still avoid a long course unless a real employer could explain what work it leads to.
fieldNote: Kira uses added time to build savings and seek **paid training** with a union role for workers.
She rejects office planning as protection from **thinking AGI**.

steps.text: Ask the union to secure paid training for crew members
Add to savings during the additional warning years
Contact nearby builders if shifts fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives workers room to plan and the union time to press for fair terms. I’d keep learning the systems that help today without calling them a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could add a lot to my savings over ten years, but AGI still reaches records in 2036 and robots reach carpentry in 2039. I don’t assume any desk or site job stays protected after those dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep working, add to my savings, and stay active in the union’s discussions. In 2037 I’d review the local work and contact other builders if my hours had dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to prepare and keep my finances steady. I’m still uneasy because the robot date reaches the craft work I’ve built my career around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dani decide before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d decide whether to buy a place or keep renting after we see what work looks like. We have no children or fixed wedding plans, so we can make that choice without a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take training if a contractor or union could show a real need for it. I wouldn’t spend the whole reserve on a certificate that claims office work is safe after AGI.

say: I’d use the decade to plan and press for **fair terms**.
I’d learn tools that help now without treating them as a **permanent shelter**.
think: I could add to savings before **2036**.
I don’t assume desk or site jobs stay **protected** after the dates.
do: Keep leading my crew while **contracts continue**.
Add to **my savings** from current pay.
Stay active in the union’s **training discussions**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the later robot date, with time to prepare.
S4.quote: I’d keep learning the systems that help today without calling them a permanent shelter.
fieldNote: Kira uses the decade for **savings and worker voice**, not a safety claim.
She and Dani leave a home decision open while their **work outlook develops**.

steps.text: Keep leading my crew while contracts continue
Add to savings from current pay
Stay active in union discussions about training and notice
Decide with Dani whether to buy or keep renting before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years gives little time before the office work changes and robots arrive around 2031. Paid training, clear notice and a worker voice in staffing decisions would help me plan without assuming my savings can carry me forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask who pays for training when the tools change. Workers should not have to choose between a paycheck and keeping up with the system their employer selects.

headlineQuote: Workers should not have to choose between a paycheck and keeping up with the system their employer selects.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** crew lead with high earnings and a strong trade reputation.
She lives with Dani and has a **strong savings reserve**.
She values familiar craft work but supports **worker voice** and union involvement.
Her savings and many nearby builders help, while robots still threaten **hands-on carpentry**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Kira most because the short warning leaves little time before robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training and clear notice** would help Kira plan while workers have a voice in staffing decisions.
